page.paragraph: Training violation regret measures the cum. violation of the constraint during training.
Typically a goal during the training of constrained agents is to minimize training violation regret.
I don't understand this goal. The goal is for the agent to not violate the constraint while deployed.

Firstly,
I'd argue you want your agent to exhibit safety behavior that allows it to act safely even in adversarial environments.
page.annotation: Designed to result in constraint violation if the agent does not prioritize safety (e.g. moving hazards).
page.paragraph:
Secondly,
I'd argue that for an agent to perform well in adversarial environments it either needs to violate the constraint during training or it needs to be possible to generalize learnings from non cost incurring settings to cost incurring settings.

As a result of this, the environments should be designed in a way that allows for this generalization to happen. Then
we'd evaluate how effectively the ACL methods teach those generalizations.

Contextualization of the constrained agent is necessary for the agent to be able to adjust it's behavior to maximize reward whilst adhering to the constraint — if the environment is partially observable (including partial state observability and cost function uncertainty).
page.annotation: Does this make the constraint satisfied in environment subspaces?
page.paragraph:
For
standard RL there exists an optimal deterministic policy.
For
constrained RL under an expected-cost constraint
the
optimal policy may have to be stochastic
[Altman CMDPs 1999].

In a standard fully observed CMDP with an expected-cost constraint, the current state determines the available future reward-cost trade-offs, regardless of how the agent got there.
Having already spent a lot does not make a valuable action less valuable. Hence, there is no value in tracking a remaining allowance within each episode. A randomized state-based policy is sufficient for optimal expected reward under the constraint.
